en: Many were the men who went;
None came back again.
Gray mist descends and veils its cliffs.
Forty sorcerers from China,
The infidels' wonders, have settled there.
Those Chinese wonders—
No man has stepped across to them;
Whoever challenged them did not survive;
No man has drawn near;
Whoever drew near did not remain alive.
There are deeply dug pits;
There are salt flats to trudge through.
The Russian khan, Kerki Khan,
Has ten thousand champion troops.
No living creature can escape
The net of iron ropes he possesses.
For whoever goes to that forest,
He has misery boiling.
Those Chinese wonders—
My foal, I shall tell you their secret now.
Whoever meets them will not go unharmed.
Their tigers have borne fifteen litters.
That suck human beings in,
Their dragons number sixty.
On the farther side
They have sword-trunked elephants.
To go to the forest is a hellish undertaking;
Know this, my precious son!
On the farther side
Are forty thousand troops from China.
When they sweep down in force,
No one escapes by the slightest movement.
Such a perilous road it is:
No ridge to rush toward headlong,
No place for making sport.
There are dragons and elephants;
That chew human beings up—
There are fanged beasts as well.
There are many different tales.
If a person is seen in the forest,
He has a single eye in his head.
Your father, your Temir Khan,
Has these many words to tell you.'
He says it each day and will not leave it be;
Temir Khan says it at night as well.
Never giving up hope in these words,
Temir Khan says it every day.
When he hears this news,
Will he turn his steed's head away?
The only son of your falcon—
Will he refrain from flying his hawk?
Could the little one fail to grow excited,
And stand quietly, as though struck down by God?
He who set grassy lands alight,
Who burned the meadows,
Who poured blood into clear water,
Who cut off a head when told to take a hat,
Who drank poison when told to drink water—
Told to spill blood, he spilled stomach filth.
Blood-shedding Manas's only son
Heard Temir Khan's words:
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoy—
He heard, 'Good heavens, those who visit never return!'
'That forest standing there,
I shall scout all around it.
If from the Russians or Chinese
An enemy comes out to fight,
I shall slaughter them all.
I shall scatter its dragons and elephants,
And open a road through the forest.
Entering the forest,
Filling the pits they have dug,
If a dense host comes from the bank,
If a giant comes with brows fixed in wrath,
If embers come through gray mist,
If mighty bullets come,
I shall fight without sparing my life,
Battle all the way to Altay,
And wreck and scatter their camp.
I shall crush the enemy he names,
Extinguish the fire they have lit,
And all this Bukhara
I shall move away together.
Worn out with his worries,
My aged father Temir Khan—
I shall settle the frightened one there too.
I shall make my dear self a lion.
All the robbers
I shall crush and drive away,
And make Kul-Tokoy my home.
If an enemy comes from the Russians,
If I do not drive them as far as Ombu,
If a Chinese enemy comes from Beijing,
If I do not drive them as far as Kakan,
If an enemy comes from the Muslims,
If I do not drive them into Mecca,
Until the supple stalks ripen,
Until autumn gossamer flies,
Fighting fiercely for six full months,
If I do not gather all the surrounding peoples,
If an enemy comes out shooting,
If I do not drive and shatter them,
And slaughter every one of them,
May I perish as though never born!
While young, for my people,
Rather than go lumbering about,
Let me look upon Judgment Day.
Bloody slaughter, burning embers—
Would a true man stand and watch?
Would a prince's son
Stand in fear of death?
One of the seven days brings death.
What God has marked out,
Must not the mortal on loan endure?'
Galloping from the palace, gathering speed,
Speaking these frenzied words,
He put on his shot-proof armor.
The Boz Kise Kanykei had given
He fastened tightly at his waist.
A helmet of blue iron
He lifted and placed on his head.
That drum and crescent axe
He took up and arrayed himself.
All his weapons of war,
The darling left by the tiger
Fastened each in its proper place.
The gold-cheeked crescent axe
He fitted snugly at his wrist.
His undiminishing ammunition
He lifted and loaded upon his horse.
He hurriedly said his prayers,
Saddled Aktulpar,
And left Bukhara in a frenzy,
Yielding neither to Ysmayyl
Nor to Temir Khan,
Have you heard of him,
The offspring of the unyielding hero?
The mount beneath him
Was Temir Khan's courser;
What he held in his hand
Was Ysmayyl's falcon.
Leaving Bukhara behind,
That marvelous one touched by saints
Loomed like Opol Mountain.
Taking the slanting mountain path,
Your poor one touched by Khizyr
Loomed like a blue mountain spur.
Hurrying and hastening on the road,
Sparing no horse, he traveled far.
Without looking around,
Or thinking, 'If a rival foe appears,
What will become of this ocean-like head?'
He thought of nothing at all.
The darling kept traveling onward,
Upon the courser beneath him
Laying the whip right and left.
The reckless boy kept traveling,
Sparing no horse, he traveled far.
Without sparing himself, he traveled,
Semetey did not stop to hold back.
Drawing near broad Ak-Chiy,
Along the single path beside it,
Again the mighty orphan boy
Skirted the edge of Ak-Chiy,
And roamed about May-Bulak.
His elder sister Kanykei,
When the poor woman was a maiden,
Would go out for pleasure
To sacred Keng-Kolchuk.
Drawing near Keng-Kolchuk Mountain,
Onto Keng-Kolchuk's broad ridge
The boy came up.
Below, through dusty haze,
He saw gray scrubland.
Its corners loomed through the haze,
Its edges took shape dimly.
Here and there within it
Plane trees as large as houses showed.
When he saw those plane trees,
The boy's heart was stirred.
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoy—
Its forest was a fine place.
It had ridge upon rugged ridge,
And rough mountain passes.
Hill upon hill formed its ridges,
Its passes ran through foothills.
'My father calls the lower part Kul-Tokoy.'
Into Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoy
He entered laughing.
There were scattered marshes;
Within that forest
Geese flew singly.
Pintails teemed, stirring the water,
Red-headed ducks bobbed,
The cranes cried out;
When its other cranes called,
They clamored like women whose husbands had died.
There was snow upon its mountains,
There were rooks in its forest,
There were creatures of every kind.
The one God had created
Such a forest as this,
Fashioning it into a wondrous dwelling.
Its birds hatched in the birches—
Good heavens, they were preparing to fly!
Its birds hatched in the poplars,
Eagerly bestirring themselves to fly.
Its red plane trees were as large as houses;
Over and over came the cries
Of its sweet-voiced snowcocks.
Even after sixty days of enjoyment,
One would never have one's fill,
Of the delight of this forest.
Its cuckoos raise their melodies,
Calling from every willow.
When the cuckoos sing their songs,
A grieving soul can scarcely bear to hear,
Yet cannot move a handspan outside.
Its nightingales sing until dawn;
Their voices take a thousand forms.
A sorrowful soul can scarcely bear to listen;
All those burdened with grief
Cannot leave this forest.
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoy
Was a place for laughter and delight,
Every wondrous occupation—
A place to learn it and take pleasure,
A place where a true man
Could do what he knew and take pleasure,
Where a brave young man
Could remain of his own free will,
Pitching tents, tethering mares,
And settling down to camp.
Its apples ripened and became manure,
Its fallen oleaster fruit filled the ravines.
Its leaves were like tanned hide,
Its black widow spiders thumb-sized,
Its chervil thick as a wrist.
When its maral deer fled at a shout,
They were like pale cows with white blazes.
Its pheasants were like red leather pails.
It was a place to roam for pleasure.
'With sacred virtue settled here,
My father calls it Kul-Tokoy.'
Along the winding water,
Through willows that hid the sky,
The boy rode swiftly, rejoicing.
He cast off Akshumkar,
Made it seize geese and ducks,
And all his saddle straps
Were marked with geese and swans.
Skirting Kul-Tokoy,
When the saddle straps could hold no more,
He fastened them to the crupper.
His mount was Aktulpar,
In his hand was Akshumkar.
